groups.title: Authentication fundamentals: sessions versus tokens
groups.question: You are adding login to your recipe app and must choose between sessions and JWTs. Explain how each works and what it means for logging users out.

followUps.Session-based auth: server stores state,: How does session-based authentication work, and how do you log someone out?
followUps.JWT-based auth: stateless tokens with HM: Why is revoking a JWT harder than revoking a session?

evidence.text: The server stores a session record and sends the browser a cookie with the session id.
On each request the browser sends the cookie and the server looks up the session.
Deleting the session on the server logs the user out immediately.
A JWT contains the user's identity and is signed so the server can verify it was not changed.
The server does not need to store it, so each request is checked by verifying the signature.
A valid JWT works until it expires, so short expiry and refresh tokens are used to limit the risk.

misconceptions.text: Says a JWT's contents are encrypted and cannot be read without the secret.

groups.title: Password security and token storage
groups.question: Your user table leaks in a breach, and separately an XSS bug lets an attacker run scripts on your site. Explain how password hashing and cookie settings limit the damage.

followUps.bcrypt's adaptive cost factor and per-pa: Why use bcrypt with a salt and cost factor instead of a fast hash?
followUps.HTTP-only cookies prevent XSS from steal: How do HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite cookie flags protect the session?

evidence.text: A random salt makes identical passwords produce different hashes.
The cost factor makes hashing deliberately slow, so guessing passwords takes far longer.
The cost can be raised over time as computers get faster.

misconceptions.text: Says passwords should be encrypted so they can be decrypted when needed.

evidence.text: HttpOnly cookies cannot be read by JavaScript, so XSS cannot steal them.
Secure cookies are only sent over HTTPS.
SameSite limits sending the cookie on cross-site requests, which helps against CSRF.

notEnough: Only saying cookies are safer than localStorage.

groups.title: Implementing auth in Express and React
groups.question: You are writing the sign-up, login and auth middleware for your Express API. Explain how passwords are stored and checked and how protected routes know who the user is.

followUps.bcrypt.hash and bcrypt.compare for passw: How do bcrypt.hash and bcrypt.compare work at sign-up and login?
followUps.JWT auth middleware: verify Bearer token: What does a JWT auth middleware do on each request?

evidence.text: At sign-up the password is hashed with a cost factor and only the hash is stored.
At login bcrypt.compare checks the typed password against the stored hash.
You never compare passwords or hashes with a plain equality check.
It reads the token from the Authorization header.
It verifies the signature and expiry, rejecting the request if invalid.
It attaches the decoded user to the request for later handlers.

notEnough: Only saying it checks the token.

groups.title: Role-based access control and React route guards
groups.question: Admins can delete any recipe, regular users only their own, and signed-out users who open /dashboard should be sent to login and then back. Explain how you would enforce this on the server and in React.

followUps.Express middleware for role-based author: How would a requireRole middleware work, and what does it not cover?
followUps.ProtectedRoute wrapper in React Router v: How would a ProtectedRoute redirect to login and then back to the original page?

evidence.text: It runs after authentication, once the user is known.
It checks the user's role and returns forbidden if it does not match.
Rules like 'only your own recipe' need a separate check against the record itself.

notEnough: Only saying it checks if the user is admin.

evidence.text: It reads the auth state and renders the page only for signed-in users.
Otherwise it redirects to the login page.
It passes the original location so login can send the user back afterwards.

notEnough: Only saying it blocks the route.

misconceptions.text: Says a frontend route guard alone keeps the data secure.
